title.en: The Man Who Went Out to Search for His Son

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The man who went out to search for his son', eBook #28932

summary.en: Searching the coasts for a son lost in his kayak, a wizard-father outfaces a giant whose drum-skin is human belly, killer-whale helping spirits, a ravine man-eater he turns on his own legs, a moss-stopped seal bone that asks a favour, a mussel luring him to the bottom, and a boot-drying ogress felled by word-magic. The last stranger shows him his son's kayak skin, stretched out — the boy has been eaten — and the father tramples the man-eater's bones to nothing.
summary.zh: 父親沿海尋找失蹤之子：先後挫敗欲吞他的鼓皮巨人（殺人鯨靈助破屋救主）、誘他入深谷的食人巨漢（反将其摔落）、求他拔出孔中青苔的海豹骨、誘他下海的蚌精、以及靴子掛高的老嫗（一句咒語使其斃命）。最後一名生人展示晾曬的皮——正是兒子的皮艇皮——孩子已被吞食；父親將食人者踐踏至骨碎。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Cannibalism motifs presented as told in the archival source.

passages.text: In the days of the forefathers, a man went out along the coasts searching for his son, who had gone out in his kayak and not returned. One day he saw a giant beside a great glacier and rowed up to him; entering the giant's house, he was shown a beautiful drum with a skin taken from the belly of a man — and the giant trembled all over with the desire to eat him. Great salmon began dropping down through a hole in the roof, and the frightened guest could not get out of the place; but being a great wizard he called upon his helping spirits: 'Killer whales, killer whales — come forth, my helping spirits and show yourselves, for here is one who desires to eat me up.' They came forth, the house was crushed, the giant killed, and the man rowed on in search of his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who went out to search for his son'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He met a second big man who did nothing but eat men and threw their kayaks down a great ravine. 'Come here and look,' said the man-eater, leading him to the deep ravine and trying to thrust him backwards into it — but the man caught the giant's legs and cast him down instead. Rowing on, he heard the bone of a seal calling to him: 'Take away the moss which has stopped up the hole that goes through me,' and did so. A mussel at the bottom of the sea cried for him to row his kayak straight down through the water to visit it — but that mussel wanted to eat him, and he did not heed it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who went out to search for his son'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day he saw an old woman and rowed up to her. 'Let me dry your boots,' she said — and hung them up so high he could not reach them, so that he could not sleep for fear. It was revealed she was a man-eater; he got hold of his boots and fled to his kayak with her running behind: 'If only I could catch him, and cut him up' — and the kayak nearly upset, so strong were her words. 'If only I could send a bird dart through her,' said the man, and as he spoke the woman fell down on her back and broke her knife. He rowed on and met a stranger who said, 'See what a skin I have stretched out here' — and he knew at once it was his son's kayak: the stranger had eaten his son. The man went up on land and trampled the man-eater to death, so that all his bones were crushed, and went home again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who went out to search for his son'; not verbatim.

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Atungait, who went a-wandering', eBook #28932

summary.en: The great Atungait picks the strongest woman at the football ground — a small player who alone can knead his double-thick ribbon-seal skin — and drives off with her through strange lands: up a sheer rock he bores his own footholds, past the all-left-handed, the man-eaters who eat one another, and the lame, copper-ajangat-playing people whose stolen plaything he rescues by trailing sole-leather that swallows their pursuing rock-ridges. Flying home, he finds his wife rubbing noses with a stranger, kills her for lying, spares the honest stranger, and marries the strong woman.
summary.zh: 阿通蓋特在足球場上挑中力氣最大的女子——小個子卻能揉軟他特製的雙厚環斑海豹皮——一同駕犬出遊。途中他徒手在絕壁上鑿階登頂，犬隊循跡而上；歷經全用左手的部落、互相吞食的食人族、以及賴銅環戲的跛足者——搶走銅環戲後，以拖地的皮底誘使追來的岩脊沉入冰中。他飛回家中，見妻子與陌生人磨鼻，因她撒謊而殺之，饒了誠實的陌生人，轉而娶了那位強女。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Killing of the lying wife presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Atungait, that great man, had a fancy to go on a sledge trip with a strong woman. He had a ribbon seal flayed, forbidding his wife to scrape the meat side clean so that the skin might be as thick as possible, and dried it. In winter he visited a tribe well known for its football, marked the one strongest among the players — a woman small of stature who always contrived to snatch the ball from the others — and gave her the great thick skin to knead soft, which no other woman could have done. He took her on his sledge and drove off wandering through the lands around.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atungait, who went a-wandering'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They came to a high steep rock rising from open water; Atungait sprang up on it and began running up, so strong that at every step he bored his feet far down into the rock. He called to his dogs, and one by one they followed by the way of his footsteps — all save one, which died. Then he hoisted up his sledge and his wife and drove on. They passed a place of people who were all left-handed; then man-eaters who ate one another, having no other food, but could do him no harm; then people who had one leg shorter than the other from birth, lying on the ground all day playing ajangat, with a fine plaything made of copper. Atungait stayed some time, and when he set out, stole their plaything and destroyed all their sledges; the lame ones, unable to pursue, dealt magically with rocky ridges, which rushed over the ice towards the travellers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atungait, who went a-wandering'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Hearing something like the rushing of a river, Atungait turned and perceived rocks rolling towards him. 'Have you a piece of sole-leather?' he asked his wife, and she tied it to a string to drag behind the sledge; when the stones reached it they stopped suddenly and sank down through the ice, while the lame ones cried behind: 'Bring back our plaything, and give us our copper thing again.' Longing for home and not knowing where they were, Atungait flew off through the air — for he was a great wizard — found his house, looked in at the window, and saw his wife rubbing noses with a strange man. 'Huh! You are not afraid of wearing away your nose, it seems.' She rushed out; 'You have grown clever at kissing,' he said; 'No, I have not kissed any one,' she cried — and Atungait grasped her roughly and killed her, because she had lied. The stranger came out and admitted the truth, and Atungait let him live because he spoke it. After that he flew back to the strong woman and made her his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atungait, who went a-wandering'; not verbatim.

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Kumagdlak and the living arrows', eBook #28932

summary.en: Ill with a bad leg in his lonely tent, Kumagdlak sees enemies land from umiak and kayak. His arrows tremble of themselves, for their points are men's shinbones and their master is uneasy; as a great wizard he can breathe life into them so they fly and kill alone, and his mother's child-carrying pouch thong turns every enemy arrow wide. The taunt about tasting the water of the dead is answered: his first arrow flies over the boats, the second cuts the old leader's bowstring and pierces him, and the living arrows win the battle before a conjured storm drowns the rest.
summary.zh: 瘸腿獨居的庫馬格拉克見敵舟登岸。他的箭簇由人脛骨所製，因主人不安而自行顫動；身為大巫，他呵氣即可賦箭生命，使其自飛殺敵；幼時母親攜兒袋的皮帶一揮，敵箭盡皆偏飛。老者譏他將『飲地下亡者之水』，他以活箭回敬——首箭越船而過，次箭截斷老人弓弦、穿其身而歿；群敵潰逃，他再喚風暴，令殘敵盡葬海底。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Arrows of men's shinbones and the breath-given life of weapons are documented wizard-lore.

passages.text: Kumagdlak lived apart from his fellows, with his wife the only living being beside himself. One day, looking for stones to build a fireplace, she saw many enemies approaching over the sea: 'An umiak and kayaks,' she cried. Her husband lay in the house with a bad leg, ill at ease. 'My arrows — bring my arrows!' he cried, and his wife saw all his arrows lying there trembling, because their points were made of the shinbones of men, and they trembled because their master was ill at ease. Kumagdlak, feathering them with birds' feathers, was a great wizard: by breathing with his own breath upon those arrows he could give them life, causing them to fly towards his enemies and kill them; and when he stood unprotected, he grasped the thong of the pouch in which his mother had carried him as a child and struck out with it, and then all arrows aimed at him flew wide of their mark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kumagdlak and the living arrows'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The enemies hauled up on shore, and the eldest among them cried out: 'Kumagdlak! It is time for you to go out and taste the water in the land of the dead under the earth — or perhaps you will go up into the sky?' 'That fate is more likely to be yours,' answered Kumagdlak. Standing at the entrance of his tent he knew that if but the first arrow could be sent whirling over the boats, none of them would be able to harm him. The arrow flew over the boats; the next cut through the string of the old speaker's bow and pierced the old man himself. Then, his wife handing him the arrows as he shot, he began shooting down the others; the men from the boats shot at him, but all their arrows flew wide, and his enemies, growing fewer and fewer, at last fled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kumagdlak and the living arrows'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Kumagdlak took all the bodies down by the shore and plundered them, taking their knives; and when the boats had got well out to sea, he called up a great storm, so that all the others perished. The waves washed the bodies this way and that along the coast until the clothes were worn off them. Here ends the story of the man who, lame in his own house, was yet beyond the reach of the weapons of the living.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kumagdlak and the living arrows'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Giant Dog of the Hills

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Giant Dog', eBook #28932

summary.en: A childless man owns a dog big enough to haul whales and narwhal ashore, hooking the narwhal on its side teeth; thongs through holes in its jaws steer it, and the amulet meant for his son — a knot of hard wood — makes it hard for death to come at it. It crushes three bear-sized dogs, then takes to hunting the inland-dwellers and dragging home their legs, hairy-booted, in its jaws — and from that giant dog, the teller says, the inland folk got their great fear of all dogs.
summary.zh: 無子的男人養著能拖鯨上岸的巨犬——一角鯨咬在它的側齒上，頜穿孔中的皮繩可供操縱；本該給兒子的護身符（硬木結）令它難以死去。巨犬咬碎三隻熊般大的敵犬，又慣於獵殺內陸人、拖回毛靴之腿獻給主人——內陸人見犬便懼的天性，正是從這隻巨犬而來。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The inland-dwellers (tornit) are the legendary giant folk of Greenlandic tradition.

passages.text: There was once a man who had a giant dog: it could swim in the sea, and was so big it could haul whale and narwhal to shore, hooking the narwhal on to its side teeth and swimming with them hanging there. The owner had cut holes in its jaws and let in thongs, so that he could make it turn either way by pulling at them; when he and his wife wished to journey anywhere they had only to mount on its back. He had long wished for a son, and as none was born, he gave the great dog the amulet his son should have had — a knot of hard wood — and the dog was thus made hard to resist the coming of death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Giant Dog'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Once the dog ate a man, and its owner had to leave the place and settle elsewhere, hiding it in the hills and keeping it busy with a great bone whenever a stranger's kayak came in. Its size and fierceness made him many enemies: once a stranger drove in with a sledge drawn by three dogs as big as bears, to kill the giant dog; it pretended to be afraid at first, but when the stranger's dogs set upon it, it turned and crushed the skulls of all three in its teeth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Giant Dog'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In time the man noticed his dog going off on long journeys into the hills and sometimes returning with the leg of an inland-dweller — he could tell by the hairy boots — and understood the dog had made it a custom to attack the inland folk and bring back their legs. From this giant dog, the teller says, the inland-dwellers got their great fear of all dogs: it would appear suddenly at the window and drag them out. But it was a good thing something frightened the inland-dwellers, for they had themselves an evil custom of carrying off lonely folk, especially women, who had lost their way in the fog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Giant Dog'; not verbatim.

region.zh: 西北格陵蘭伊塔（史密斯海峽）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Inland-dwellers of Etah', eBook #28932

summary.en: A dog-team scents out an inland-dweller's house by the great lake east of Etah; the terrified tornit thrust out an old woman, who dies of fright at the dogs. The visitor apologizes; they answer that her skin was already wrinkled and it does not matter — then flee far up country, never to be seen, their house remains yielding only a single narwhal tusk. The inland-dwellers are not really dangerous, only shy and dog-fearing: one coast woman's tornit husband bled from the eyes at sight of dogs, and their runners' swiftness is trained inside a worm-filled ribbon-seal skin that sucks their blood and lightens their feet.
summary.zh: 犬隊循跡至伊塔以東大湖畔的內陸人之屋；驚恐的托尼特人推出一名老婦，老婦見犬嚇死。來人致歉，答曰『她的皮本已皺了，無妨』——隨即舉族遠遁深山，自此絕跡；屋基中只掘出一支獨角鯨牙。內陸人本無危險，只是怯懦怕犬：海濱女子蘇瓦克的內陸丈夫，一見犬便雙目滲血；其飛毛腿訓法，是將人縛入填滿蠕蟲的環斑海豹皮中，吸盡血液，使腳下輕快。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Tornit (inland-dwellers) ethnogenesis material; note also documents death of the old woman as told.

passages.text: A sledge drove round to the east of Etah, up into the land near the great lake; suddenly the dogs scented something and dashed off over a great plain, then checked and sniffed at the ground — the entrance to an inland-dweller's house. The inland-dwellers screamed aloud with fear when they saw the dogs, thrust out an old woman, and hurried in to hide; the old woman died of fright at the sight of the dogs. The man went in, very ill at ease because he had caused the death of the old one: 'It is a sad thing that I should have caused you to lose that old one.' 'It is nothing,' answered the inland-dwellers, 'her skin was already wrinkled; it does not matter at all.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Inland-dwellers of Etah'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The sledges drove home, but the inland-dwellers were so terrified that they fled far up into the country and have never been seen since; the remains of their houses were all that could be found, and when men dug there for more, nothing came up but a single narwhal tusk. The inland-dwellers are not really dangerous, the teller explains — only shy, and very greatly afraid of dogs: there was a woman of the coast-folk, Suagaq, who took a husband from among the inland folk, and when that husband came to visit her brothers, the blood sprang from his eyes at sight of their dogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Inland-dwellers of Etah'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The tornit train themselves to become swift runners so that they may catch foxes. When an inland-dweller is to become a swift runner, they stuff him into the skin of a ribbon seal filled with worms, leaving only his head free; the worms suck all his blood, and this, they say, makes him very light on his feet. There are still some inland-dwellers left, but they are now gone very far up inland.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Inland-dwellers of Etah'; not verbatim.

title.en: Neruvkaq, Who Stabbed His Wife in the Leg

region.zh: 西北格陵蘭納齊維利克（史密斯海峽）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The man who stabbed his wife in the leg', eBook #28932

summary.en: Neruvkaq torments his inland-dweller wife Navarana, stabbing her leg with an awl, until she flees to her many brothers. They storm his roof, losing one leg at the joint; he decks himself in a child's tunic sewn all over with walrus tusk that no one can kill, puts his sealskin coat on the dog as a decoy, leaps to the great meat-stone — footprints still on it — and shoots his enemies down while his mother strengthens him by magic. But the frightened Navarana will not come out from under the bench, and chews the walrus meat he thrusts in to her until she dies there — 'the old sneak!'
summary.zh: 內魯瓦克以錐刺妻子納瓦拉納的小腿取樂，她終投奔內陸的眾兄弟。兄弟們踏其屋頂，一足被切於膝；他穿上縫滿海象牙的幼時舊衣——著之者無人能殺——以犬著皮外套誘敵，縱身躍上分肉巨石（足印至今猶存），其母以巫術助力，亂箭退敵。然而嚇破膽的納瓦拉納再不肯出長凳之下，啃著丈夫塞入的海象肉，最後死於其處——『那老膽小鬼！』

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Domestic violence presented as told in the source; the closing taunt is the teller's own.

passages.text: Neruvkaq's wife Navarana was of the tunerssuit, the inland-dwellers, their only sister with many brothers, and they lived at Natsivilik, the place with a great stone where men lay out meat. Neruvkaq was cruel to his wife: he would stab her in the leg with an awl, and when the point reached her shinbone she would snivel with pain. 'Do not touch me; I have many brothers,' she said, but as he did not cease ill-treating her she ran away to those brothers at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who stabbed his wife in the leg'; not verbatim.

passages.text: All the many brothers moved down to Natsivilik, sprang upon the roof of Neruvkaq's house, and began to trample it; one thrust his foot through, and Neruvkaq's brother cut it off at the joint — 'He has cut off my leg' — and the brother-in-law hopped about on one leg until the blood was gone from him and he died. Neruvkaq hastened to put on a tunic worn as a little child, made larger from time to time and covered all about with pieces of walrus tusk: none could kill him as long as he wore that. He put the sealskin coat on his dog and thrust it out as a decoy — the brothers outside stabbed the dog to death, taking it for him — and jumped to the great meat-stone, so strongly that his footmarks are seen on the stone to this day; there he took his arrows all barbed with walrus tusk and began shooting his enemies down, his mother giving him strength by magic means.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who stabbed his wife in the leg'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon but few enemies were left, and they fled away southward, fleeing and fleeing without stopping until they had gone a great way. Navarana, now afraid of her husband, crept in under the bench and hid; she would not come out again, so her husband thrust in a great piece of walrus meat, and she chewed and gnawed at it to her heart's content. 'Come out, come out, for I will never hurt you any more,' he said — but she had grown so afraid of him that she never came out any more, and so she died where she was at last: the old sneak, the teller calls her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who stabbed his wife in the leg'; not verbatim.

title.en: Avovang: The Soul That Lived in the Bodies of All Beasts
title.zh: 阿沃萬格：寓於百獸之魂

region.zh: 東格陵蘭康格盧克蘇瓦克峽

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts', eBook #28932

summary.en: Avovang, whom nothing could wound — enemies stab at him standing on his child-wrapping dog-neck skin, and drag him to a cliff he refuses to fall from — is finally shoved through a seal breathing-hole by men who covet his southern wife. His soul, wanting to know the manner of every beast's life, becomes seal, fox, dog, reindeer, wolf, walrus, and raven in turn, learning each creature's gait and food, and avenges itself on its murderers as a seal that drowns them and a fox that wrecks their sledges — until a nail-less toe fells it at last, and the soul creeps into a woman's body to be born again as a man.
summary.zh: 刀槍不入的阿沃萬格——敵人屢刺不傷，拖上懸崖也摔他不死——終被覬覦其南地妻子的同伴自海豹呼吸孔推入海中。其魂為遍歷百獸之生態：先化海豹、狐狸復仇，淹死撞毀仇人；再為偷食之犬、逐群之鹿（『後腿向天邊踢出』）、追獵之狼、潛底之海象、腳寒之鴉；末了重為海豹，卻栽在一個剪去大趾甲的獵人手裡。魂自手套鑽入婦人之身，轉世重為男子。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Soul-migration through animal bodies is core Inuit cosmology; the tale doubles as natural-history teaching.

passages.text: There was a man named Avovang, of whom it is said that nothing could wound him; he lived at Kangerdlugssuaq. One nearing-summer day, when his brother stood by a seal's breathing hole, a sledge dashed up with the warning that many sledges would come to kill his brother; the brother hid away up a steep rocky slope. The sledges drove up before the house, and Avovang went out to meet them carrying the skin of a dog's neck that had wrapped him as a child; standing on that piece of skin, he could not be wounded though the men stabbed again and again. Mockingly he told them his body was now like a piece of knotty wood with the scars of their wounds. Dragged to the top of a high cliff to be cast down, he changed himself each time into another man who was not their enemy, until they were forced to drive away without having done what they wished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He desired once to travel south to buy wood, as men were wont in the old days, and took a wife from among the people of the south on that journey. While the men stood looking for seal breathing-holes they all felt a great desire to possess Avovang's wife, and tried to kill him: Qautaq stabbed him in the eyes, and the others sent him sliding down through a breathing hole into the sea. His widowed wife, so angry she broke all the wood they had brought from the south into small pieces, went home. Then a great seal rose in the sledges' path, and many fell through the thin ice and were drowned; then a fox lured them up a mountain of screw-ice and dashed them down, so that only two escaped. It was the soul of Avovang that had changed first into a seal and then into a fox, bringing about the death of his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Afterwards he made up his mind to let himself be born in the shape of every beast on earth, that he might one day tell his fellow-men the manner of their life. He was a dog, eating what men threw away and tired at last of the many beatings; a reindeer, taught to kick out towards the farthest edge of the sky at the gallop and to eat moss and lichen, growing fat with suet; a wolf, taught 'Kick up towards the sky' so he could overtake the reindeer and get food; a walrus, taught to swing his hindquarters up to the sky to dive, and fed on mussels and little white stones; and a raven — 'The ravens never lack food, but they often feel cold about the feet.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last he became a seal again and lay under the ice watching the men who came to catch him; being a great wizard he could hide himself under the nail of a man's big toe. But one day a hunter who had cut off the nail of his big toe harpooned him; hauled up on the ice and cut up in the house, Avovang went with the mittens the man cast to his wife and crept into the body of the woman — and after a time he was born again, and became once more a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts'; not verbatim.
